title: How Agritourism Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain agritourism (agri-tourism): farms attracting visitors to observe or take part in farm life. They open with a true-crime setup about Ronald Levins Sr. and Jequita Evans, Florida labor camps that used crack and inflated company-store prices to hold workers in debt bondage. They then cover drivers of agritourism (factory farming, industrialization, globalization, farm income below about fifty thousand dollars a year), the consumer desire to reconnect with farms and food sources (citing Robert Lamb's HowStuffWorks article), the three levels of agritourism (supplementary, complementary, primary), and types: direct marketing, education and experience (Serenbe apprenticeships, Maverick Farm in North Carolina), and recreation/event agritourism (corn mazes, pumpkin patches, Homeplace at Land Between the Lakes, Conner Prairie's Follow the North Star). They discuss community supported agriculture (CSA), repeat visits, a Tennessee Tech agritourism degree, and Colorado economic statistics, then close with listener mail.

entities.name: Homeplace by the Lakes National Recreation Area

segments.title: Opening banter and Facebook plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about pre-record banter and ask listeners to like the show's Facebook page, then set up the episode topic.

segments.title: Florida labor camp setup story
segments.summary: Josh recounts how Ronald Levins Sr. and Jequita Evans ran Florida labor camps that recruited homeless workers, used a company store with inflated prices and crack to put workers in debt, and were prosecuted, as a contrast to agritourism.

segments.title: Definition of agritourism and examples
segments.summary: Chuck defines agritourism as attracting visitors to observe or take part in a farm business, with a winery example. The hosts discuss the film Sideways and a viral grape-stomping video.

segments.title: Why farmers turn to agritourism
segments.summary: Chuck explains that factory farms dominate production while most farms are small, and that many farms earn under fifty thousand dollars a year, so farmers diversify. Globalization adds competition, and the hosts joke about it.

segments.title: Consumer demand and reconnecting with farms
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Robert Lamb's article on reconnecting people with their food, the decline of rural life, farm-to-table, and visiting ancestral farms.

segments.title: Supplementary, complementary, and primary agritourism
segments.summary: Three levels are described: supplementary (small add-on income), complementary (roughly half and half, such as pumpkin patches), and primary (the farm's main income is visitors).

segments.title: Types of agritourism: direct marketing, education, recreation
segments.summary: Direct marketing such as roadside stands is covered; education and experience examples include Serenbe's apprenticeship and Maverick Farm's bed-and-breakfast work stay in North Carolina; recreation and event agritourism covers festivals, corn mazes and living history at Homeplace and Conner Prairie's Follow the North Star program.

segments.title: Repeat business, CSAs, and the Tennessee Tech degree
segments.summary: Agritourism aims for repeat visits. Community supported agriculture (CSA) boxes are described, along with McQueen Orchard as a personal example and Tennessee Tech's agritourism degree.

segments.title: Economic statistics and wrap-up of topic
segments.summary: Colorado reports two point two billion dollars in agritourism economic contribution and 13.2 million visitors; the 2007 US Census of Agriculture figures are cited. The hosts doubt the Colorado figure and mention wineries and breweries as agritourism.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck read listener gifts and letters, including coffee, shirts, soaps, postcards and CDs, plus promotions for various sites, and close the show.
